assumptions: Assumes the backend stores or processes relationship mappings for invitation and access control.

title: Invitation action may be persistently logged with attribution
description: The backend is likely to log that a specific parent initiated an invitation for a specific secondary guardian at a certain time. Such attributable logs create evidence of the parent's action and can reduce deniability.
assumptions: Assumes standard backend audit or security logging for account-sharing/invitation events.
uncertainty_note: Logging is typical for invitation/account-sharing events, but the precise retention and attribution details are not provided.

title: Invitation may process personal data of additional data subjects beyond the primary service user
description: This flow introduces processing of personal data about an additional adult (the secondary guardian) and ties that person to the child and parent. If the feature requests or transmits more information about the invitee than necessary to deliver the invitation, it increases disclosure risk across more data subjects.
assumptions: Assumes invitee personal data is submitted as part of the invite flow.
uncertainty_note: The flow inherently involves another data subject, but whether this exceeds functional necessity depends on the exact invite design.

title: Child location access is propagated to a dynamically determined additional party
description: The purpose of this flow is to grant or prepare access for a newly invited secondary guardian to view the child's location. This makes the child's personal data accessible to an additional, dynamically selected party, increasing disclosure exposure if not tightly constrained.
assumptions: Assumes a successful invitation results in the secondary guardian obtaining access to the child's location data.

title: Child may lack transparency about disclosure of location to an added guardian
description: When the backend processes an invitation for a secondary guardian, the child's location data may become accessible to another adult without the child being adequately informed in an age-appropriate way. This creates a risk of covert or insufficiently transparent disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the child is a data subject in the service and may not receive clear notice when additional viewers are added.
uncertainty_note: Whether notice is provided to the child is not specified.

title: Granting a secondary guardian access to child's location may be unlawful without proper authorization
description: Sharing a child's location with an additional guardian may require a valid lawful basis, proper parental authorization, and possibly child-specific safeguards. If the backend accepts invitations without adequate authorization checks, the disclosure could be unlawful.
assumptions: Assumes child location is sensitive personal data and access by added guardians requires explicit authorization controls.
uncertainty_note: Applicable legal requirements depend on jurisdiction and the product's role/consent model, but the authorization risk is genuine.

title: Invitation flow may lack adequate verification and safeguard mechanisms for secondary guardian access
description: If the backend does not robustly verify that the invited person is an appropriate secondary guardian before enabling access, the safeguard mechanism may be inadequate for protecting a child's location data and meeting regulatory expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the system may rely on a simple invite acceptance mechanism without stronger verification of the invitee's legitimacy.
uncertainty_note: The actual verification method is not described, so this is a plausible compliance risk rather than a confirmed design flaw.

title: Linking child and guardian identities through shared live-location access
description: Granting a secondary guardian access to the child's live location creates an explicit relational link between the child's location stream and a specific guardian account/role. This enables data about different individuals (child and guardian) to be linked through the sharing relationship.

title: Secondary guardian can identify the child from location-sharing context
description: The shared live-location payload and its metadata/context reveal which child is being tracked, even if the flow description does not state that a direct name is sent. Identity can be inferred from the guardian relationship and the location-sharing context.
uncertainty_note: The exact identifiers present in the payload are not specified; this threat is grounded in likely identity-revealing context/metadata rather than confirmed explicit identifiers.

title: Backend may create attributable logs of guardian access and location-sharing events
description: To grant access and share live location, the backend will typically log the authorization and delivery events with timestamps and account identifiers. Such records can create evidence that the child location was shared with a specific secondary guardian, reducing deniability for involved parties.
uncertainty_note: Logging is common for authorization and access events, but the existence and retention of such logs are not explicitly stated in the flow description.

title: Observation of live-location updates can reveal when tracking is active
description: Because the backend shares the child's live location with the secondary guardian, network-visible request patterns or update timing could allow an observer to detect that location tracking and guardian access are active, even if message contents are protected.
uncertainty_note: This depends on network visibility and traffic-analysis feasibility; encryption and transport protections are not described.

title: Sharing live location may disclose more precise location data than necessary
description: Providing a child's live location to a secondary guardian may expose highly fine-grained, continuously updated location data. If the functional need is only general whereabouts or emergency visibility, real-time precise coordinates would exceed the necessary granularity.
uncertainty_note: The flow description says 'live location' but does not specify precision, update rate, or whether this level of granularity is strictly required.

title: Continuous live-location sharing may process data more frequently than necessary
description: Live-location sharing implies repeated or continuous transmission of the child's location to the secondary guardian. This may exceed the frequency needed for the intended function, especially if periodic or on-demand access would suffice.

title: Child location is disclosed to an additional predetermined party
description: The backend makes the child's location accessible to a secondary guardian, expanding disclosure to another known external party. This increases exposure and may exceed the minimum set of parties necessary for the service.

title: Child may be unaware that live location is being disclosed to a secondary guardian
description: The flow describes backend sharing of the child's live location with a secondary guardian. If the child is not given age-appropriate transparency about this disclosure, the sharing constitutes covert or insufficiently transparent processing from the child's perspective.
uncertainty_note: The description does not specify whether the child is informed through UI notices or policies.

title: Child may lack effective control over secondary-guardian location sharing
description: Once the backend grants the secondary guardian access, the child may have limited ability to intervene, revoke, or constrain the scope of live-location sharing. This creates a risk of insufficient intervenability and control over the disclosure.
uncertainty_note: No information is provided about revocation, pause, or consent controls.

title: Sharing a child's live location with a secondary guardian may lack valid lawful basis or required consent
description: Disclosing a child's live location to a secondary guardian is high-risk processing of children's personal data. If the backend grants this access without an appropriate lawful basis, authorization, or required parental/guardian consent mechanism, the flow may be unlawful.
uncertainty_note: Whether the secondary guardian is properly authorized is not stated; legality depends on jurisdiction and the app's consent/guardian-verification design.

title: Guardian authorization or safeguard mechanism may be inadequate for child-location sharing
description: Granting secondary-guardian access to a child's live location may require strong verification and safeguards to ensure the recipient is legitimately authorized. If the mechanism for establishing or verifying secondary-guardian status is weak, the flow presents a compliance risk.
uncertainty_note: The flow says access is granted, but does not describe the verification or safeguard mechanism used.

title: Aggregated analytics may still enable group profiling by the partner
description: Even if the backend shares aggregated usage and engagement analytics rather than raw user records, the receiving advertising/analytics partner can use those aggregates to profile user groups or cohorts and link behavior patterns across campaigns or datasets.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics contain cohort-, segment-, geography-, device-, or time-based breakdowns detailed enough to support group-level linkage or profiling.
uncertainty_note: The flow description says 'aggregated' analytics, which lowers direct individual linkage risk; this threat applies mainly if aggregates are segmented finely enough to enable cohort linkage.

title: Small or highly specific aggregates could enable indirect identification
description: If the backend shares analytics in narrowly defined segments, the partner may infer the identity of individuals or very small groups from a small anonymity set, especially when combined with other datasets the partner already holds.
assumptions: Assumes some shared aggregates may be broken down by sparse attributes such as region, device model, campaign, timestamp, or niche engagement segment.
uncertainty_note: No explicit identifiers are mentioned; this risk depends on whether the aggregates are sufficiently granular to shrink the anonymity set.

title: Propagation of analytics data to an external advertising/analytics partner may exceed necessity
description: Usage and engagement analytics are propagated from the app backend to an external partner for monetization of the free tier. Sharing behavioral data with a third party creates disclosure risk if the same business goal could be achieved with less or no external data sharing.

title: Behavioral analytics are exposed to a predetermined external party
description: The backend makes analytics data accessible to a known external advertising/analytics partner. Even if the recipient set is fixed, this increases exposure of user-related behavioral information beyond the primary service boundary.

title: Analytics granularity may be finer than needed for funding the free tier
description: Engagement analytics shared for advertising or monetization may include more granular behavioral, cohort, temporal, or device-level detail than is strictly necessary to support funding or reporting purposes.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include detailed dimensions rather than only high-level summary metrics.
uncertainty_note: The description does not specify the exact fields or aggregation level, so this is a plausible granularity risk rather than a confirmed over-collection.

title: Third-party analytics sharing for monetization may be insufficiently transparent to users
description: Users may be unaware that their app usage and engagement data is disclosed to an external advertising/analytics partner specifically to fund the free tier, especially if disclosures are buried or framed only generally as analytics.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether clear user notice is provided; threat included because third-party monetization sharing commonly creates transparency gaps.

title: Granularity and monetization purpose of shared analytics may be undisclosed
description: Even where users are told that analytics are collected, they may not be informed about the detail of behavioral metrics shared, the involvement of an advertising partner, or the monetization purpose behind the disclosure.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the content and clarity of notices and privacy disclosures, which are not provided.

title: External analytics sharing may lack an adequate lawful basis
description: Sharing usage and engagement analytics with an advertising/analytics partner for monetization may constitute personal-data processing or disclosure that requires a lawful basis, and possibly consent depending on jurisdiction and the nature of the analytics.
uncertainty_note: Whether this is an actual compliance violation depends on the jurisdiction, whether the data is truly anonymized, and what lawful basis or consent mechanism exists.

title: Third-party monetization sharing may violate data-minimization or purpose-limitation principles
description: If analytics shared with the partner are more detailed than necessary, or if data collected for service operation is repurposed for advertising monetization without sufficient limitation, the flow may conflict with core data-protection principles such as minimization and purpose limitation.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the actual scope of the analytics, original collection purpose, and whether strong aggregation/anonymization and governance controls are in place.

title: Check-in message and location act as a quasi-identifier for the child
description: The child's manual SOS/check-in combined with current location can be linked to the same child across events, especially within a family-safety context where the child is already a distinct subject in the system. Repeated submissions may therefore enable linking of records and behavior over time.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can associate the incoming message with the child's account, device, or family relationship.

title: Identity can be inferred from message context and metadata
description: Even if the flow payload does not explicitly contain the child's real name, the backend can infer identity from account/session metadata and the family relationship needed to route the SOS/check-in to the parent. Current location plus a child-parent context can make the child identifiable.
assumptions: Assumes the backend receives authentication, device, or account metadata sufficient to map the event to a specific child and parent relationship.

title: Backend may create attributable logs of the child's SOS/check-in
description: Processing a manual check-in/SOS with timestamp and location is likely to generate server-side records tied to the child's account or device. Such logs can form evidence that the child initiated the action at a specific time and place, reducing deniability.
assumptions: Assumes normal backend logging, audit, or event storage for message handling and delivery.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly state logging, but backend processing of safety events commonly produces attributable records.

title: Sending an SOS/check-in may be detectable from network activity
description: An observer of the child's network traffic may detect that the child has triggered a manual check-in or SOS event based on timing, destination, traffic pattern, or lack of transport protection, even if message contents are not visible.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe the child's network traffic and that traffic patterns for SOS/check-in are distinguishable.
uncertainty_note: The transport protections and traffic-shaping measures are not specified.

title: Precise current location may disclose more granularity than necessary
description: The child sends current location together with a manual check-in/SOS. Depending on the intended functionality, highly precise location may exceed what is strictly needed to notify the parent that assistance or attention is needed, increasing privacy exposure.
assumptions: Assumes exact coordinates or similarly fine-grained location are transmitted rather than a coarser area.
uncertainty_note: The description says 'current location' but does not specify the precision or whether exact location is strictly necessary for SOS handling.

title: Child may not be aware of location granularity and use of SOS data
description: In a child-focused context, the child may not fully understand how detailed their transmitted location is, how the backend processes the SOS/check-in, or how long it is retained and shared with the parent. This creates a risk of inadequate awareness of the scope and purpose of processing.
assumptions: Assumes transparency is provided primarily through the app and may not be age-appropriate or sufficiently specific about granularity and downstream handling.
uncertainty_note: The flow description alone does not state what notices or UX disclosures are presented to the child.

title: Potential data-minimization and transparency compliance risk for child's location processing
description: Processing a child's manual SOS/check-in together with current location can create compliance risk if the backend collects more location detail, retains it longer, or uses it for broader purposes than necessary for the parent-notification function. Because the data concerns a child, minimization and transparency obligations are especially sensitive.
assumptions: Assumes applicable child/privacy regulation and that the backend stores or further processes the event beyond immediate delivery.
uncertainty_note: Specific jurisdiction, lawful basis, parental-consent mechanism, and retention practices are not provided, so this is framed as a potential compliance risk rather than a confirmed violation.
